nameStory: Catnip gets its name from the intense, almost magical attraction that about two-thirds of cats have to this plant. The scientific name 'cataria' comes from medieval Latin, reflecting its long-standing association with our feline friends. When cats encounter catnip, they often roll, rub, and act absolutely euphoric thanks to a natural chemical called nepetalactone.
description: Catnip is a gray-green, fuzzy herb in the mint family that grows 1-3 feet tall with the characteristic square stems of all mints. Its soft, heart-shaped leaves have scalloped edges and feel almost velvety to the touch. Small white or pale purple flowers bloom in spiky clusters at the stem tips during summer. This short-lived perennial has a distinctive musky-minty scent that's unmistakable once you know it.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that are distinctly four-sided when you roll them between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, gray-green, heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges that feel fuzzy and almost velvety to touch, arranged in opposite pairs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale purple two-lipped flowers clustered in dense spikes at stem tips, blooming from June through September

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Distinctive musky-minty fragrance when leaves are crushed - not as pleasant as culinary mint, with an almost medicinal quality

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms bushy clumps 1-3 feet tall, often looking somewhat scraggly with multiple branching stems from the base

habitat: Catnip thrives in disturbed soils along roadsides, field edges, abandoned lots, and waste places throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, somewhat dry soils in full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy herbs like plantain, chicory, and other non-native mints.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy gray-green shoots from the ground, with young leaves being especially soft and aromatic.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and bloom from June through September with their characteristic flower spikes. This is peak identification season when all features are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin setting small three-sided seeds. Leaves may yellow but often retain some green color into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds. Look for small nutlets on the ground near where plants grew.

funFact: Catnip contains the same mosquito-repelling compounds found in some commercial insect repellents, making it about 10 times more effective at repelling mosquitoes than DEET - so while your cat is having a party, you're getting natural bug protection!
confusionNotes: Catnip is often confused with other members of the mint family, but its fuzzy gray-green leaves and musky scent set it apart from the brighter green, more pleasantly scented culinary mints. Remember: if it smells good enough for tea, it's probably not catnip!
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'catmint,' true catnip (Nepeta cataria) is different from ornamental catmints often sold in garden centers, which may not have the same effect on cats. The plant's sedative properties have made it popular in herbal teas for humans, earning it folk names like 'catswort' in medieval England.
compareHints: Since catnip is the only Nepeta species commonly found wild in New England, compare it to other mint family members. Unlike spearmint or peppermint with their bright green, smooth leaves and pleasant scent, catnip has distinctly fuzzy, gray-green foliage and a musky odor. Wild bergamot is taller with showier flowers, while ground ivy stays much lower and has kidney-shaped leaves.
